scenes.narration: This slide is about creating replaceable EC2 instances rather than hand-maintained pets. On the left, an Amazon Machine Image supplies the operating system and initial software configuration. A versioned launch template adds instance type, networking, storage, IAM instance profile and user data settings. The two work together, but they are not the same artifact. Move to the upper-right user data panel. Bootstrap scripts can prepare an instance, but they need retry handling and should not embed long-lived credentials. Repeatable prepared images are another valid approach when startup speed matters. Next, inspect the instance profile and IMDSv2 security panel. Instance roles provide temporary AWS credentials, and requiring IMDSv2 helps protect metadata access where supported. Finally, the bottom-right panel makes a crucial operational point: changing a launch template version does not modify already running EC2 instances. You must roll new replacements, preferably behind health checks, using a suitable deployment or Auto Scaling process. The architectural goal is an auditable baseline and a safe replacement procedure that can be repeated after instance loss.

scenes.title: Stateless compute: make replacement safe
scenes.visual_overview: The slide depicts stateless compute: make replacement safe through labeled architecture panels and a visual takeaway.
visual_walkthrough: Trace session and durable state moving outside an individual EC2 instance
Explain shared databases, caches and storage plus their own resilience needs
Distinguish rebuildable temporary files from irreplaceable local state
Follow load balancer to multiple AZs and replacement capacity

scenes.narration: The central orange EC2 instance is surrounded by replacement arrows. Those arrows represent a desired operating property: instances should be disposable without losing important data. Start at the upper-left panel. User sessions and durable business state should not be trapped on one server's local disk or memory. Move to the upper-right, where shared databases, caches and object or file storage can keep state outside the instance. These dependencies require their own durability, resilience, availability and consistency design; moving the data does not automatically make it safe. The lower-left panel distinguishes temporary files and caches that can be rebuilt from irreplaceable application state. If deleting an instance destroys a critical upload or business transaction, replacement is not yet safe. Finally, follow the load balancer in the lower-right panel to workloads across multiple Availability Zones. Multiple instances only help when the common database and dependencies remain available and replacement capacity can launch. The goal is a stateless application tier with deliberate externalized state, not merely more EC2 servers.

scenes.narration: This is a four-way purchasing decision, but the slide warns us to separate price discounts from guaranteed EC2 capacity. Start at the left. On-Demand suits flexible usage with no long-term commitment, while Savings Plans and eligible Reserved Instances offer discounts in exchange for commitments and matching rules. The next panel is the common mistake: a regional Reserved Instance discount does not by itself guarantee capacity in a specific Availability Zone. The third panel identifies options when capacity assurance matters, such as eligible zonal Reserved Instance reservations and On-Demand Capacity Reservations. These have conditions and costs that must be evaluated independently from the discount. Finally, the orange Spot panel explains the tradeoff of unused capacity at discounted rates: Spot instances can be interrupted, so they suit fault-tolerant work that can checkpoint, retry or redistribute. For exam architecture, assess the workload's tolerance for interruption, its demand predictability and whether it needs assured placement. Then choose the pricing or reservation mechanism that actually meets those requirements, rather than assuming the largest discount provides availability.
